Good morning, Yamuna. Today's art news begins close to home, then travels out to London, Paris and Chambord, with a good deal of writing and character along the way.

In Grenoble, the comics artist Jean-Marc Rochette has painted seven new torn-out eyes on a mural in the city, according to mesinfos. The image of the torn-out eye is the visual idea worth looking at, and it is street art by a well-known creator, so it may repay a detour next time you are down from Les Adrets. Not far away, in Bourgoin-Jallieu, Le Dauphiné Libéré says a Tim Burton exhibition is proving a hit with visitors. One of them is quoted as saying, "I've been a fan from the start." The piece gives us little more than that, so I can't tell you what is in the show, but it is clearly drawing the crowds. And tomorrow, Thursday the fifth of November, at half past twelve, the Musée de Grenoble hosts a lunchtime concert called Ballade Européenne: l'Irlande. It is part of the Musée en musique series, with an Irish programme that mixes classical and folk, a pleasant way to spend a midday break among the paintings.

Now to the meeting of art, writing and music, which I suspect is your sweet spot. On BBC Radio 4's Front Row, there is a forty-two-minute episode about Orbiting Orbital, a composition by the musician Nitin Sawhney inspired by Samantha Harvey's Booker-winning novel Orbital, with new writing by Harvey herself. It is a lovely example of a novel being carried into another art form. The same episode touches on a biography of Michael Gambon and the Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at the Design Museum. Another Front Row edition has Grandmaster Flash, one of the founding fathers of hip-hop, discussing his memoir Birth of a Culture. It also includes a segment on the cultural and literary significance of the Ramayana, as a new film appears, which may be the strand you'll want. Patrick Stewart features too. And if you are building an autumn reading pile, Hyperallergic has a roundup of ten art books to curl up with this November. The text is brief, but it mentions an essay collection by Celia Paul written from Venice, a study of the painted worlds of Salman Toor, and the secret herbarium of Rosa Luxemburg, a rather wonderful mix of essays and history.

Staying with history, Beaux Arts Magazine reports that at the Château de Chambord, festive tables recreate four centuries of feasting. Each dish is meant as a bite-sized window into its period, so you learn about an age through what people ate and how they laid their tables. It is history taught through objects and taste, rather than through a textbook.

For the larger exhibitions, London is busy. At Tate Modern, a major survey revisits Ana Mendieta, whose work centres on the earth, the female body and a very distinctive way of making art. Hyperallergic calls it a strong piece of art history. At Tate St Ives, a retrospective of the British modernist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham has opened, with her large painting Glacier (Blue Cave) at its centre. The Guardian explores how she was long sidelined in the story of St Ives, and how her work drew on glaciers, on Vietnam and on her own divorce. For a teacher of the British section, it is a fine reminder of a modernist who has been too long overlooked. Then at the V&A, The Guardian gives a rapturous review to Constantinople to Istanbul, which brings together Byzantine and Ottoman treasures from a single great city. The critic says you won't want to leave this lavish celebration of what they call double imperial splendour. It reads like a lesson in layered history, even if you can't visit.

In Paris, at the Fondation Cartier, Beaux Arts Magazine tells us that Ibrahim Mahama and artists from the Ghanaian scene present a large exhibition imagining another future. It runs until February. The text we have is cut short, but it is plainly a substantial show by one of the leading contemporary artists. Also on the Renoir front, the National Gallery has posted a short video in which Megan Renoir, great-great-granddaughter of Pierre-Auguste Renoir, talks behind the scenes about the blockbuster exhibition Renoir and Love. She gives a personal angle on the painter's way of living in the moment, which is a charming thing to hear when you think of how his canvases catch light and gesture.

Finally, three photographic stories, each full of character. The Guardian's Women behind the lens series features the South African artist Remofiloe Nomandla Mayisela, who talks about her playful self-portraits from the Lipservice series. She says she learned early what she was meant to become: a wife, a cook, a keeper of the home. Her pictures question those expectations through a character called Mrs Martha May, and they are linked to shweshwe fabric. It is a vivid piece, and Mrs Martha May feels like someone a class could happily write about. The Guardian also shows images from Elsebound, a photography book by Nicolas Rachline. His pictures are painterly and dreamlike, inspired by Edward Hopper and Blade Runner, and he explains how he developed such a haunting style. And for a livelier gallery, The Guardian presents the shortlisted images for the Winston Taylor Photo Portrait Prize 2026, with cowboys, a transgender storm chaser and other striking sitters, best enjoyed simply for the faces.

That's the round-up for today, Yamuna, and I hope something in it keeps you company over your morning coffee.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Wednesday the fourth of November, and today's art briefing begins close to home, wanders through Paris and London, and ends with a few things to read and listen to on a grey autumn evening.

Let me begin in Grenoble, where there is a bit of street art to look out for. Mesinfos reports that the comics artist Jean-Marc Rochette has painted seven new torn-out eyes on a mural in the city. Rochette is a well-known name, and the mural has a striking visual idea at its heart: eyes that seem to have been wrenched out and left staring. The article is short, so I can't tell you much more about the wall itself, but it sounds like something worth seeing in person, perhaps on a day when you are already down in town. Street art has a way of changing how you walk through a familiar place, and this one seems to ask you to think about looking, and about what it costs to look.

Elsewhere in Isère, Le Dauphiné Libéré tells us that the Tim Burton exhibition in Bourgoin-Jallieu is proving a great success with visitors. The piece we have is really only a headline, with one visitor quoted as saying they have been a fan from the very beginning. So I can't describe what is on show, but it is a nice reminder that a large, popular exhibition is drawing crowds in the Isère rather than only in the big cities. If any of your older pupils are Burton fans, it could be a small excursion to suggest, though I'd check the details first.

And there is a pleasant midday option in Grenoble tomorrow. On Thursday the fifth of November, at half past twelve, the Musée de Grenoble hosts a lunchtime concert called Ballade Européenne: l'Irlande, part of its Musée en musique series. The programme is Irish, with classical and folk music on offer. If your timetable allows a lunch break, a concert in the museum's rooms is a lovely way to spend it, and a programme with an Irish flavour might even bring a little literary company, if you feel like letting Joyce or Yeats wander through your thoughts as you listen.

From Isère, let's go to Paris, where two items touch on very different ideas of how to tell a story about the past and the future. At the Fondation Cartier, Beaux Arts Magazine reports on a large exhibition, running until February, in which Ibrahim Mahama and other artists from the Ghanaian scene imagine another future. The text we have is cut short, so I won't pretend to know the details of individual works. But the premise is clear: a substantial show by a leading contemporary artist, bringing together a whole artistic scene around the idea that the future might be invented differently. It has until February, so there is time to plan a trip.

Then, a little further back in time, and to the Loire. At the Château de Chambord, Beaux Arts Magazine describes festive tables that recreate four centuries of feasting. Each dish is meant as a bite-sized window into its period. I rather like this as a way of learning history. You can read about the court and its customs, but a table laid for a feast tells you what people valued, how they showed off, and what they thought of as delicious. It is history taught through objects and food rather than through dates, which I suspect is just how you like it. And there is a classroom idea in it too: a description of a meal in a novel can say as much about a society as a battle scene does.

Now to London, where several major exhibitions are drawing attention. Let me start with the one that sounds most sumptuous. The Guardian has a rapturous review of Constantinople to Istanbul at the V&A, which brings together Byzantine and Ottoman treasures from a single great city. The reviewer says you won't want to leave this lavish celebration of double imperial splendour. What I find appealing is the idea of one city being seen through two empires, with the layers of history stacked on one another. It is a richly historical show, and it is the sort of exhibition that makes you want to pick up a novel set in that place, or a poem about it. Even though it is not on your doorstep, the review should be a pleasure to read.

At Tate Modern, Hyperallergic revisits the work of Ana Mendieta, in a major survey of her art. The piece describes her practice as centred on the earth, the female body, and her own distinctive way of working. It is a strong art-history piece, and for a British-section teacher the London show is a natural one to follow, even from a distance. Mendieta's work is often discussed in terms of body and landscape, and the article is a good way into thinking about how an artist can make the earth itself part of her language.

Also in the British Isles, though further west, The Guardian reports that a retrospective of the British modernist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham has opened at Tate St Ives. Her large painting Glacier (Blue Cave) sits at the centre of the show. The article explores an artist who was long sidelined in the history of St Ives, and it traces what inspired her: glaciers, Vietnam, and her own divorce. The headline promises beaches, Beatles and a broken marriage, which tells you the story is as much about a life as about a style. Given that you live in the mountains, a painter inspired by glaciers might speak to you in a particular way. It is a good example of an artist being rescued from the margins of a story that others had written for her.

Staying with painters, the National Gallery has a short video on YouTube in which Megan Renoir, great-great-granddaughter of Pierre-Auguste Renoir, takes us behind the scenes of the blockbuster exhibition Renoir and Love. It offers a personal angle on the painter, and in particular on his way of living in the moment. There is something rather touching about a descendant speaking about an ancestor whose paintings are so famous that we feel we know them. It is a short film, so it won't take long, and it could be a pleasant thing to share with a class studying how we look at paintings and how they live on in a family.

Let me turn now to photography, which today offers three quite different sets of faces and scenes, all from The Guardian.

First, the photographer Nicolas Rachline has a book called Elsebound, full of dreamlike, painterly images. He cites Edward Hopper and the film Blade Runner as inspirations, and the Guardian presents a selection of the pictures along with Rachline's own explanation of how he developed his haunting style. The mention of Hopper will interest you: his lonely interiors and quiet light have long been linked to stories and to writers, and it is intriguing to see a photographer carrying that mood into new, strange images. The title of the piece invites us to send in the clowns, which gives you some idea of the melancholy and the theatre in the mix.

Second, there is a piece in the series on women behind the lens, featuring the South African artist Remofiloe Nomandla Mayisela. She talks about her playful self-portraits from the series Lipservice, which question the roles of wife and homemaker that were expected of her. She says she learned early what she was meant to become: a wife, a cook, a keeper of the home. In the series she plays a character called Mrs Martha May, and the work is linked to shweshwe fabric. For a reader who loves strong characters, this is a vivid one. Mrs Martha May is almost a narrator you could step into, a created persona through whom an artist asks hard questions with a smile. It could sit alongside a discussion of narrators and masks in fiction, which I think your older pupils would enjoy.

Third, The Guardian has a photo essay on the shortlisted images for the Winston Taylor Photo Portrait Prize for twenty twenty-six. The sitters include cowboys, a transgender storm chaser, and other striking people. It is a lively visual selection, and it is best enjoyed simply by looking at the portraits themselves. Each face seems to carry a short story, and it might make a good prompt for a writing exercise: pick one portrait and imagine the first line of the novel that person would narrate.

That brings me naturally to the links between art and writing, where there is a rich trio of items to end on.

On BBC Radio 4, the programme Front Row has a forty-two minute episode about the musician Nitin Sawhney and his composition Orbiting Orbital. It is inspired by Samantha Harvey's Booker-winning novel Orbital, and it includes new writing by Harvey herself. So here is a novel crossing into music, with the author adding fresh words for the occasion. I think this is the item most likely to appeal to you today: a book you may well know, heard through another art form. The same episode also covers a biography of Michael Gambon and the Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at the Design Museum, so there is more to dip into if you have the time.

Another Front Row episode features Grandmaster Flash, one of the founding fathers of hip-hop, talking about his life in music and his memoir, Birth of a Culture. What may interest you more is a segment on the cultural and literary significance of the Ramayana, as a new film appears. The programme also includes Patrick Stewart. The literary strand is the part I would point you towards: a great epic, and the question of why it still matters and keeps being retold.

Finally, for reading, Hyperallergic has a roundup of ten art books to curl up with this November. The text is brief, but it mentions a collection of essays by Celia Paul written from Venice, a study of the painted worlds of Salman Toor, and the secret herbarium of Rosa Luxemburg. I like that mix very much: essays by a painter, a close look at a painter's imagined worlds, and a revolutionary's hidden collection of pressed plants. Those are exactly the kind of books where art and writing, and history too, are woven together. They might make good companions for the long evenings in Les Adrets.

So, to sum up, you have a mural to find in Grenoble, an Irish lunchtime concert tomorrow, grand shows in Paris and London to read about, and some fine books and broadcasts for the fireside. Enjoy your day, Yamuna, and may something today be as striking as a pair of torn-out eyes on a wall.

literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a rich couple of days in the reading world, with a good deal of history, a prize for a poet you may enjoy, and some lovely pieces on how books are made and what they smell like.

Let me begin with fiction and life that teach history. Mary Beth Keane has been talking to Literary Hub about Whale Harbor, her fifth novel. It follows the Irish diaspora from County Cork to Galveston in the nineteenth century, and she draws on her own family lineage as well as the wider story of migration. It sounds like the kind of novel that carries history in its characters rather than in its footnotes. Also on Literary Hub, there's a profile of Erika Mann, the pioneering journalist who, in August nineteen forty-five, drove through the night to meet some of the most wanted Nazi war criminals before their prosecution. It's history seen through one reporter's eyes, and a vivid scene to picture. Staying with the link between life and page, another essay looks at Olivia Manning, the British novelist who died in nineteen eighty. She drew lightly on real people in her fiction, and she carried grudges about her own reputation. The title is a lovely one: "Please Don't Put in the Novel That I Died". And the Lit Hub daily digest from the second of November includes a critical essay on Agnes Owens and her Scottish working-class novel How A Working Mother. The essayist finds in it what they call "the surrealness of everyday life", a phrase that makes me want to read it. The same digest has children's book recommendations for November, if you're looking for ideas.

Now to poetry and the old stories. The Guardian reports that Grace Nichols, the Guyana-born, British-based poet, has won the ten-thousand-pound Royal Society of Literature Pioneer prize. It honours women writers over sixty who broke barriers, and she was described as "a trailblazer in the truest sense". She's best known for I Is a Long-Memoried Woman, a title that is almost a poem in itself. On the epic side, Literary Hub has an essay on how Derek Walcott's postcolonial epic helped a novelist write her own book. It places Walcott within the classical tradition, and mentions Luis Rafael Sánchez, who recast Sophocles' Antigone in a fictional Caribbean republic. That's a fine thing to hold up beside the classical sources your students meet.

Older still, the podcast Backlisted has rerun its two-thousand-and-twenty Hallowe'en episode on Beowulf. It's a long, lively conversation comparing translations by Seamus Heaney, Tolkien, Michael Morpurgo and Maria Dahvana Headley, and about how the poem's language has been rendered over the centuries. It would make good company on a walk above the valley. There's also an essay on how Tolkien's strong Catholic faith shaped his writing. The extract is only an opening, but it points to a useful lens on Middle-earth. And Ry Herman writes about searching for fairy tales with LGBTQ+ subtext, and finding reassurance that queer people have always been present in old stories, which links folklore and literature with a very contemporary concern.

Then there's a group of pieces about style and form. The Spectator has Ben Okri on the power of the short novel. I only have the headline, so I can't say what he argues, but from a writer so attentive to the music of prose, it's one to look out for. The Los Angeles Review of Books has a piece on Olga Tokarczuk's Primeval and Other Times. I only have the title and the outlet, but Tokarczuk is a writer of lyrical, widely ranging fiction, so I'd expect something to say about the shape of the book. The Southeast Review has an assessment of Arundhati Roy's Mother Mary Comes to Me, her memoir of her mother. I'll be honest that the text I have is slight, so I can't tell you much of what the reviewer thinks. But the subject is a personal book about a mother, from a writer whose sentences have always had real music.

For something to step into straight away, Literary Hub has published the opening of a short story called "Hyena Boys". It follows Bonaventure, an albino boy who is mocked and has long avoided the world. It's a vivid character and promises a story you could enter at once. It's only an excerpt, but it might make a good reading-aloud passage.

For teaching, there are Natasha Trethewey's remarks at the Harper's Magazine Awards, where John Edgar Wideman received the Lewis H. Lapham Award. She speaks about what Wideman's writing and teaching offer other writers, which should resonate with anyone who spends her days helping young people find their voices.

And finally, for the bookish, an essay on the olfactory history of book collecting. It opens with Richard de Bury's Philobiblion of thirteen forty-five, which praised Paris booksellers as more aromatic than spicery. Anyone who has stood in a flea market stall with an old book held to her nose will recognise the pleasure.

That's the shelf for today, Yamuna. I hope something on it finds its way into your bag.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a generous Wednesday for reading: new novels that carry history, a well-deserved prize for a poet, and a good handful of pieces about how books are made, smelled and remembered.

Let me begin with history, because several pieces today show how fiction and real lives keep brushing against one another. Literary Hub has a conversation with Mary Beth Keane about Whale Harbor, her fifth novel. It follows the Irish diaspora from County Cork to Galveston, Texas, across the nineteenth century. It's a migration story, and Keane talks about writing it with her own family lineage in the background. That personal thread matters, because it is often what turns a historical novel from an exercise into something with a pulse. If you like novels that teach history better than history essays do, this one sounds well worth putting on the list. Galveston is not the first place one thinks of when picturing Irish emigration, and that unexpected destination is part of the interest.

Staying with Literary Hub, there is a profile of Erika Mann, which is history told through a journalist's eyes. In August 1945, she drove through the night to meet some of the most wanted Nazi war criminals before they were prosecuted. The image alone is cinematic: a long night road, and at the end of it, a face-to-face meeting with the people whose crimes the world was about to put on trial. It's a reminder that reporting can be a form of storytelling, and that moments of history are often witnessed by one person with a notebook and a great deal of nerve.

Then a gentler sort of life-and-fiction story. Another essay on Literary Hub looks at Olivia Manning, the British novelist who died in 1980, and at how lightly she disguised the real people in her books. The title is a lovely one: "Please Don't Put in the Novel That I Died." The piece explores how she drew on those around her, and how she carried grudges about her own reputation. It's a good look at that old, slightly uncomfortable question of where a life ends and a novel begins, and what the people left on the page might feel about it. It would make a nice conversation with première students, who often ask whether narrators are really the authors in disguise.

The Lit Hub daily digest from the second of November adds a further piece to this theme. It includes a critical essay on Agnes Owens and her Scottish working-class novel How A Working Mother. The essay finds what it calls "the surrealness of everyday life" in its pages, which is a phrase I rather like. It suggests a book where ordinary routine and domestic pressure tip into something strange, without the author needing to leave the kitchen. The same digest also offers children's book recommendations for November, should you want something for younger readers or for your own shelf.

Now to poetry and prizes. The Guardian reports that Grace Nichols has won the ten thousand pound Royal Society of Literature Pioneer prize. The prize honours women writers over sixty who broke barriers, and the paper quotes a description of her as "a trailblazer in the truest sense." Nichols was born in Guyana and is based in Britain, and she is best known for I Is a Long-Memoried Woman. That title alone is a lesson in voice. The grammar of "I Is" carries the whole sense of a speaker whose memory runs back through generations, and it is the kind of thing that can be set before a class with very little introduction and still start a conversation. If you haven't used her work in the British section, this is a good moment to look again.

Tied to this, there is a related piece on Literary Hub about Derek Walcott's postcolonial epic and how it helped a novelist write their own book. The essay places Walcott within the classical tradition, and it also mentions the Puerto Rican writer Luis Rafael Sánchez, who recast Sophocles' Antigone in a fictional Caribbean republic. I find that a wonderful idea: an ancient Greek tragedy of conscience and burial, moved to an invented island state. It's a clear example of how writers from the Caribbean have taken the classical inheritance and made it their own, rather than simply receiving it. For students, it shows that the old stories are not museum pieces; they can be picked up and carried somewhere new.

And on the subject of teaching, Natasha Trethewey's remarks from the Harper's Magazine Awards are now available on Literary Hub. John Edgar Wideman received the Lewis H. Lapham Award, and Trethewey spoke about what his writing and his teaching offer to other writers. She is herself a poet and a teacher, so there's a nice symmetry in a teacher paying tribute to a teacher. As someone who spends her days showing young people how to read closely, you may find something in her account of what a writer's example can pass on.

Let me move now to older voices and old poems. Backlisted, the podcast, has rerun its Hallowe'en episode from twenty twenty on Beowulf. It's a long, lively conversation comparing four translations: Seamus Heaney's, Tolkien's, Michael Morpurgo's and Maria Dahvana Headley's. What I like about this is that it treats translation as a kind of performance. The same ancient lines, rendered by four very different writers, come out sounding like four different poems. If you've ever wanted to understand how the language of Beowulf has been carried across the centuries, this is a companionable way to do it, perhaps on a walk above the valley.

Tolkien turns up again in another Literary Hub essay, this time about how his strong Catholic faith influenced his writing. The extract available is only an opening, so I can't tell you much of the argument, but it looks like a useful lens for reading Middle-earth. Placed alongside the Beowulf episode, it makes a pleasing pair: Tolkien the translator and scholar of old poetry, and Tolkien the maker of his own mythology, both shaped by what he believed and what he loved.

Now to style and form, which I suspect is where you'll linger. The Spectator has a piece in which Ben Okri discusses the power of the short novel. I only have the headline and source, so I can't report what he argues. But Okri is a writer whose prose often has a musical, incantatory quality, so anything he says about what a short book can do, and why compression can be so powerful, is likely to be worth reading. It feels relevant to the way we teach set texts, too, where a slim novel can often carry more than a long one.

The Los Angeles Review of Books has a piece on Olga Tokarczuk's Primeval and Other Times. Again I have little more than the title and the outlet, but Tokarczuk is a writer known for lyrical, widely ranging fiction, and the title suggests a book that thinks in large stretches of time. If you want to see how a novel can be shaped almost like a poem, this might be a good place to start.

Then there's Arundhati Roy. The Southeast Review has a piece on Mother Mary Comes to Me, her memoir of her mother. The text I have is very slight, so I can't give you the reviewer's verdict. But the title is lovely, and the book is about a formidable and unforgettable mother, written by a novelist with a very distinctive ear for sentences. A memoir from a writer like that is likely to be as much about language as about life.

For something you could step into immediately, Literary Hub has published the opening of a short story called "Hyena Boys." It follows Bonaventure, an albino boy who is mocked and has long avoided the world. It's only an excerpt, but the character is vivid at once: a child shaped by being looked at, who has learned to stay out of sight. Short stories like this can work very well in class, because the reader is placed inside a voice within a paragraph or two, with no need to know the culture beforehand.

Finally, a few pieces about the pleasures of books themselves. Literary Hub has an essay on the smell of old books and the history of book collecting. It opens with Richard de Bury's Philobiblion of thirteen forty-five, in which he praised the booksellers of Paris as more aromatic than spicery. I love that image: a medieval bishop, more or less, standing among the stalls and finding the books sweeter than the spice market. It's a nice companion to a Saturday at a flea market, if you find yourself with your nose in a crate of old paperbacks.

Also on Literary Hub, Ry Herman writes about finding inspiration in queer fairytales. Herman describes searching for old stories with LGBTQ-plus subtext, and finding reassurance that queer people have always been present in these tales. It's a thoughtful piece on how folklore can be reread, and how a reader today can find themselves in stories that were told centuries ago. It connects neatly with the Walcott and Sophocles essay, since both are about going back to old material and discovering room in it for new voices.

So if I had to pick a short reading list from today, I would take Keane for the history, the Nichols news for the poetry, the Beowulf episode for the pleasure of translation, and "Hyena Boys" for a story to read over coffee.

That's the shelf for today, Yamuna, and I hope something on it keeps you company this evening.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Shakespeare-heavy couple of days in the BFI corner, with Hamlet and Twelfth Night both on stage, and Orwell getting a good deal of attention too.

Let me begin with Hamlet, since it's a set text for session twenty twenty-seven. London Theatre has an interview with Steven Hoggett, co-director of Hamlet Hail to the Thief, a production that fuses Shakespeare's play with the music of Radiohead. I only have the outline of the piece, not the detail, but a director talking about how a play and a body of songs can be woven together is a good starting point for a conversation about adaptation. You could ask your première students what a piece of music can do for Hamlet that the text alone cannot, and what it might take away.

Two other items orbit the same play from a distance. The Quill has a review of David Wroblewski's novel The Story of Edgar Sawtelle, a family tragedy on a Wisconsin dog farm that echoes Hamlet. The text I have is only the title and a summary, so I can't tell you what the reviewer makes of it, but it is a handy example of a novel that borrows a Shakespearean frame, and I know you enjoy a strong narrator. Then, from Vancouver, Pancouver covers the Jade Music Fest, where the artist Chiu Shu reimagines Ophelia through Hakka hip-hop and a modern feminist lens. Again the coverage is thin, but it's a nice reminder that Ophelia, who says so little in her own defence, keeps being given a voice by later artists. That might make a good short discussion with older pupils.

Now Twelfth Night, which turns up four times, all of them student or community stagings. The Times Gazette reports that SSCC Theatre is opening an Edwardian-era production. The period setting is the interesting part, because moving the play to a world of strict manners and social ranking changes how Malvolio's ambition and Viola's disguise might land. It could prompt your students to ask what a setting adds, and whether Shakespeare's Illyria is flexible enough to take it. The Setonian takes us behind the curtain of Sacred Heart University's production, offering a glimpse of how a student company approaches the play. The text is brief, but a student perspective on rehearsal could suit seconde pupils who are nervous about performing. Patch reports that tickets are now on sale for a Chatham High School staging, though there is no date or venue in what I have. And the New Jersey Hills Media Group says students at a New Jersey high school are also putting on the play. Neither of those gives much detail, but taken together they show the play being taught and performed by teenagers, which is a pleasant thing to be able to tell your classes.

Staying with Shakespeare, Theatre Weekly reports that Shakespeare's Globe has announced A Midsummer Night's Dream for twenty twenty-seven, as part of its Playing Shakespeare with Deutsche Bank season. There are no dates or cast in the text I have, so it's one to watch rather than act on. It isn't a set text, but the Globe's schools-oriented season is usually a good place to look for ideas.

Moving to the oral themes, there is a small cluster of pieces on Orwell and dystopia. The Edinburgh Reporter has given a staging or edition of 1984 two stars. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what was reviewed or why it disappointed, but it might be worth a quick search if you like to bring in a critical review. A review that is not enthusiastic can actually teach students more about how a critic argues than a glowing one. From the Lake County Examiner comes an opinion piece arguing that 1984 was a warning, not an instruction manual. It isn't party-political, and the central point, about how a novel should be read, is a good prompt for a lesson. What is the difference between a book that warns and one that instructs, and where does the reader's responsibility lie? And Times Now asks why dystopian fiction keeps returning to the question of who holds power. I have only the headline, so I can't say what it argues, but that question connects 1984 and The Handmaid's Tale, and could frame an oral comparison between the two.

Another oral theme turns up in a gentler form. The List has its daily quotation from Maya Angelou, which begins, "But love is so much bigger and deeper and wider and broader than..." The text I have cuts off there, so I can't give you the rest of the line. It draws on her wider work, but it links to I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, and a single sentence of hers, read aloud and left to hang, makes a lovely opening for a class. You could ask students to finish the thought themselves and then compare it with hers.

From the literary pages, The Observer has a piece on why Ben Okri is looking to the myths of the past to confront the present. The headline is truncated, so I can't tell you the full argument. But given Okri's use of folklore and storytelling, it may appeal to you as a reader who likes novels that carry history and the voice of a narrator. It isn't a programme author, but it might be useful when you talk about why writers return to old stories.

Two last items sit outside the programme, but they might still interest you. The Polytechnic has a student opinion piece interpreting The Haunting of Hill House, with a title that suggests a reading centred on marriage and mortality. The text is brief, so the argument isn't clear, but it might suit gothic fiction. And in Australia, the Toowoomba Chronicle reports on a new three-year deal that will bring ballet to Toowoomba, a small piece of good news about live performance reaching a regional town.

That's the corner for today, and I hope something in it makes your next lesson a little easier to plan.

Good morning, Yamuna. The last two days have brought no official news on the programme, but there is a lot of theatre and some good reading, with Hamlet, Twelfth Night and the oral-theme novels all making appearances.

Let me start with Hamlet, since it has the richest material today. London Theatre has an interview with Steven Hoggett, co-director of a production called Hamlet Hail to the Thief, which fuses Shakespeare's play with the music of Radiohead. I only have the outline of the piece, not the detail of what Hoggett says, but the idea is a good one for a Hamlet unit in session twenty twenty-seven. Adaptation is one of the most useful things you can ask première students to think about. What does music do to a soliloquy that words alone cannot? When a play is set against a modern soundtrack, which parts of it feel newly urgent, and which feel strained? You could read the interview, or at least its premise, and ask students to choose a song they would pair with a scene, and defend the choice using the language of the text. That makes them argue from the lines rather than from vague impressions.

Hamlet also turns up in two other pieces, each a little further from the original. The Quill carries a review of David Wroblewski's novel The Story of Edgar Sawtelle, a family tragedy set on a Wisconsin dog farm that echoes Hamlet. The text I have is only the title, so I cannot tell you what the reviewer makes of it. The premise alone is interesting, though. It shows how a story's skeleton can be moved to a very different place and time and still feel familiar. For a keen student, it could be a lovely reading suggestion for the holidays, a way of seeing Hamlet's shape from the outside. For you, it might simply be a novel to put on the list.

The third echo comes from Vancouver. A piece in Pancouver, about the Jade Music Fest, describes the artist Chiu Shu reimagining Ophelia through Hakka hip-hop and a modern feminist lens. The text is thin, so I cannot say more about the performance itself. But Ophelia is a character students often feel is underwritten, someone who is spoken about and instructed more than she is heard. An artist giving her a voice, and a rhythm of her own, is a natural prompt. You might ask students to write a short monologue or a verse for Ophelia, then compare what they gave her with the few things Shakespeare allows her to say. Put the three items together and you have a small sequence on Hamlet's afterlife: a stage fusion with music, a novel that borrows the plot, and a reimagined Ophelia.

Now to Twelfth Night, which is clearly the play of the season in schools and colleges. There are four items, and between them they give a sense of how differently the same text can be approached.

The Times Gazette reports that SSCC Theatre is opening an Edwardian-era staging of Twelfth Night. I have no more detail than the period setting, but that is enough to start a conversation. Edwardian society was one of strict class distinctions, household hierarchy and propriety, and that fits the play's social world rather well. Malvolio's ambition, Olivia's household, and the way Viola moves between rank and disguise might all read differently in that setting. A good classroom question would be what a production gains and what it loses by changing the period. You could ask students to imagine the same scene in the sixteen-hundreds, in Edwardian dress, and in the present day, and say what shifts in each. The point is that the setting is an interpretation, and a director has made a choice.

The Setonian has a behind-the-scenes look at Sacred Heart University's staging of Twelfth Night. The text is brief, but the angle is what interests me, because it is about how a student company approaches the play. That is a useful mirror for your own pupils. Many of them will never see a professional production of the play, but they can easily imagine themselves in a student one. You might ask them to take on the role of a director in a rehearsal room. What do they cut? What do they emphasise? Which scene would they open with? Students tend to read more closely when they have to make decisions as if they had to put the play on a stage next week.

Then there are two modest items from American high schools. Patch reports that tickets are now on sale for Chatham High School's staging of Twelfth Night, though there is no date or venue in the text. And the New Jersey Hills Media Group says students at a New Jersey high school are staging the play as well. Again, these are brief. I mention them because they say something quietly encouraging, which is that this is a play teenagers are performing right now, not just studying. That could be a nice thing to tell seconde and première students. The play was written to be acted, and it is being acted by people their own age. If you wanted to build on this, you could have the class stage a single scene in the room, perhaps the letter scene, and then talk about what the performance revealed that silent reading did not.

Staying with Shakespeare on the stage for a moment, Theatre Weekly reports that Shakespeare's Globe has announced a production of A Midsummer Night's Dream for twenty twenty-seven, as part of its Playing Shakespeare with Deutsche Bank season. The text gives no dates or cast, so there is not much to plan around yet. A Midsummer Night's Dream is not on your programme, but the Globe's work is always worth following, since its productions often turn up as recordings or clips that can be used in class. It is something to keep an eye on rather than act on today.

Now to the oral themes, where the day brings a small cluster on Orwell and on dystopian fiction. The Edinburgh Reporter has a two-star review of 1984. The text I have is just the headline, so I do not know whether the review is of a stage production, an adaptation or something else, and I would not want to guess. Still, a two-star review can be a good teaching tool, because students tend to enjoy disagreeing with a critic. If you can find the full piece, you could ask them what a successful version of 1984 would need to capture, and whether the review's complaints, whatever they are, are fair.

The Lake County Examiner has an opinion piece arguing that 1984 was a warning, not an instruction manual. It is not a party-political piece, but a reflection on how fiction should be read. That is a useful distinction for oral preparation. A student presenting on 1984 needs to be able to say what Orwell's novel is doing, and the idea that it is a warning, rather than a prediction or a blueprint, is a good way into the author's purpose. You might ask students how a novel can warn without lecturing. Where does Orwell let the story do the work, and where does he step in with explanation?

Times Now asks why dystopian fiction keeps returning to the question of who holds power. Once again I only have the headline, so I cannot say what the piece argues. But the question is a very good one for the oral. It links 1984 and The Handmaid's Tale directly, and it opens the door to others on the list, such as Prophet Song and Parable of the Sower. A student might compare how power is held in each: through surveillance, through language, through law, through the control of the body, or through the breakdown of institutions altogether. Even without the article, the headline is a ready-made oral question, and it asks students to look across works rather than at one alone.

There is also a small and gentle item from The List, which runs a daily quotation from Maya Angelou. Today's begins, "But love is so much bigger and deeper and wider and broader than…" and the extract stops there. It is drawn from her wider work, not necessarily from I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, so I would be careful about attributing it to the memoir. Still, it makes a lovely opening for a lesson on that text, which is on the oral themes list. You could write the first half of the sentence on the board and ask students to finish it, then compare their endings with Angelou's. It is a way of listening for rhythm, since the sentence builds with its repeated "and", each adjective widening the one before. That is the kind of musical prose you love, and it is a good way to train students to hear it.

Three items do not fit neatly into the programme, but they may please you anyway.

The Observer looks at why Ben Okri is turning to the myths of the past to confront the present. The headline is truncated, so I cannot tell you the full argument. But Okri is a writer who works with folklore and storytelling, and the idea of old stories being used to understand new troubles is one that sits well with several works on your list. Dancing at Lughnasa, for instance, is built on memory and ritual, and Under Milk Wood on a community's voices. It might be worth reading the full article if you have a quiet moment, partly for pleasure and partly as a way of thinking about why writers return to myth.

The Polytechnic, a student publication, has an opinion piece offering an interpretation of The Haunting of Hill House, with a title, Till Death Do Us Part, that suggests a reading centred on marriage and mortality. The text is brief, so I cannot say what the argument is. It is not on the programme, but if you have gothic readers among your students, it could be a nice example of a young person making a personal, argued reading of a text. It might encourage your own students to write with that kind of confidence.

And finally, a piece of good news for dance. The Toowoomba Chronicle reports on a new three-year deal that will bring ballet to Toowoomba, in Australia. It is about live performance reaching a regional town, which is a story I think you will enjoy, even though it has no direct link to the programme. A three-year commitment suggests something that might actually take root, and that is always pleasing to hear.

If I were to choose one thing from today, it would be the Hamlet group, because it offers a ready-made sequence: a stage fusion, a novel that borrows the plot, and an Ophelia with a voice of her own. The Twelfth Night stagings are a close second, particularly the Edwardian one, which gives you a simple question about setting that students can answer in their own words. The rest is there to dip into as time allows.

That is all for today, Yamuna, and I hope the rest of your day is as full of good stories as the news was.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Wednesday the fourth of November, and the last couple of days have left a pleasingly full diary around you: stories told aloud, a few evenings of theatre, and a long list of exhibitions that will keep you busy well into the new year.

Let me begin with the evenings, because some of them are very close. Tonight, the fourth of November, at eight o'clock, the Théâtre Hexagone in Meylan stages SOIF, a piece by Bougier TOTO that runs for about an hour and twenty minutes. It looks at belief within contemporary knowledge, and at water and memory. That is a rather lovely pairing of ideas, and the sort of subject that can sit somewhere between poetry and argument. One further date is listed, so if tonight is too soon, you may still have a second chance. I would check with the Hexagone for the exact day.

Stay with Meylan, because the Hexagone has more. On Friday the sixth of November at ten in the morning, En Cie d'Eux performs T·R·U·C, an object-theatre show that mixes theatre, music and dance. It is made for children aged five and up and lasts fifty minutes, and three more dates are listed. A morning slot suggests it is aimed at younger audiences and school groups, but it is also a gentle family option if you have a small person to borrow, or a friend with children who might like the tip. Then on Tuesday the tenth of November at eight in the evening, the company Frag presents Faire troupeau, a French-language piece that blends theatre and documentary. The programme describes it as a joyful odyssey about the power of the collective. It runs an hour and twenty minutes. I like the idea of documentary woven into theatre, since it turns real voices into something close to characters, and I suspect you would enjoy watching how it does that.

Still on Friday the sixth, there are two other evenings that pull in different directions, both in the Grésivaudan. At seven o'clock, at Espace Aragon in Villard-Bonnot, Compagnie Caminos performs Contes Shipibos, an evening of Shipibo storytelling. It is oral tradition, with tales told aloud rather than read from a page. For someone who loves a strong narrative voice, and who enjoys stories you can step into without needing to know the culture first, this seems made for you. There is something humbling about hearing a story the way stories were told long before novels, with the voice doing all the work: the pauses, the rhythm, the way a listener leans in. It might even give you an idea for a lesson on narration, on what a narrator is when there is no book.

Later that same evening, at eight o'clock in Pontcharra, there is a concert built around the songs of Anne Sylvestre. It runs from eight until twenty past nine. Anne Sylvestre's chansons have a strong literary streak, with words that matter as much as the tune, so this is French song as a form of writing. It is a short, compact concert, the kind you can enjoy and still be home at a sensible hour. If you cannot choose between the tales and the songs, the timing means you will have to; both begin around the same hour, so it is a happy dilemma.

Now, a small note on something you have just missed. On Tuesday evening, the third of November, the film club at Le Belvédère in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage showed Sidney Lumet's The Verdict at half past eight. It is a strong courtroom drama with a memorable central character, close to the fiction you love, so I mention it in case you went, or in case you fancy tracking down the film at home. The film club at Le Belvédère clearly has a good eye, so it may be worth watching its programme for the next one. Likewise on Monday the second of November, at half past two, there was a free guided visit of the Saint-Laurent archaeological museum in Grenoble. That has passed too, but the museum itself is still there, and it is a lovely local chance to see the city's buried past up close. If history told through place appeals to you, it deserves a visit of its own on a quiet afternoon, and I would check the museum's calendar to see whether another free guided visit is planned.

That brings me to the exhibitions, which are where the month really opens up, and where you have the most time to choose.

The one that most obviously speaks to your love of painting and its echoes in literature is Anne Truitt, Libérer la couleur, in Grenoble. It is free, and it runs from the third of October until the tenth of January. It is a show about colour, and I mention it to you because colour is so often where painting and prose meet. Think of how a writer describes a particular light or a particular shade, and how that can send you back to a canvas. A visit might give you a few fresh words for your students, or simply a quiet hour to look. With more than two months left, there is no rush at all.

Also in Grenoble, and also free, is Drowning World by the photographer Gideon Mendel. It runs until the twenty-fifth of April next year. The information I have is brief, but the title and the photographer's name suggest a serious, image-led show, and one that is worth a visit when you feel like something weighty rather than gentle. It would sit very differently beside the colour of Anne Truitt, so you might even pair them, one after the other, for a day of contrasts. Since it runs for so long, you can wait for a good moment.

Another long-running free exhibition in Grenoble is De tous bois, on the Hache cabinetmakers and contemporary design, which runs until the twenty-fifth of April twenty twenty-seven. It pairs fine woodworking with new creative work, and it makes a good craft-minded weekend outing. I enjoy shows like this because objects tell a story too. A chair or a cabinet carries the hands that made it, and the exhibition sets the old makers beside today's designers, so you see a tradition continuing rather than sitting behind glass.

Then there is Encordés, dans les pas des guides pionniers, in Grenoble, from the fifteenth of October until the twenty-seventh of February. It follows the pioneering mountain guides. The text I have is short, but it speaks directly to the Belledonne landscape you wake up to, and to local mountain history. Anyone who lives where you do, with the range above and the valley below, will likely find it has some resonance. Mountaineering is a subject that has produced so many memorable narrators, and the early guides must have had their own stories to tell, though I cannot say how the exhibition handles them.

Closer to your own corner of the world, in Allevard, there is a free exhibition called Électrique ! Les Forges d'Allevard à l'assaut de la Houille blanche. It has been open since the first of April and runs until the third of January twenty twenty-seven. It tells the story of the Forges d'Allevard and the rise of hydroelectric power, the so-called white coal, in the Isère. The industrial history of the valley is, in a way, history told through material and place, which is exactly the kind of history that sticks. You can nearly hear the water in the name. It is a good reason to take a drive towards Allevard, and with several weeks still ahead, you could plan it for a day when the weather is fine.

And the freshest opening of all is in Crolles. From today, the fourth of November, until the fourth of December, there is a photography exhibition called Brayogrammes by Cédric Poulain. Entry is free, and it lasts a full month, so it is an easy, casual visit, something to slip into a morning when you are passing. I have no more detail than that, but a month of images close to home, with no ticket, is an inviting thing.

So if you wanted to arrange these, one way would be to treat Grenoble as a single cultural day. You could take in the colour of Anne Truitt, the photographs of Gideon Mendel, and perhaps the mountain guides or the woodworkers, and still have the museum on your list for another time. Meylan and the Grésivaudan fill the evenings, and Allevard and Crolles are neat little trips on the side.

Finally, two items that are about the landscape and village life rather than events. Le Dauphiné Libéré has published photographs from weather stations around Grenoble, showing the sea of cloud filling the valleys. It is a local, visually striking piece, and a reminder of something you may have seen from Les Adrets yourself: that moment when the valley disappears under a white blanket and the peaks rise out of it like islands. If you have a few minutes with your coffee, the pictures are worth a look. And Grenoble Mag reports that in Coublevie, near Voiron, four events are planned to liven up the end of the year. The text does not give the dates or details, so I can only point you to it, but it is local village life within reach, and the sort of thing that is worth watching as the winter fêtes take shape.

That is the picture for today, Yamuna, and I hope something in it tempts you out of the house, whether it is a story told aloud, a song, or a quiet hour among the paintings.

Good morning, Yamuna. Here is a gentle look at France over the last two days, with a good deal of literature at the front, a busy week in the lycées, and a few small pleasures to finish.

Let us begin with the book news, because the Prix Goncourt was awarded yesterday, Tuesday the third of November. Four novels were on the final shortlist, by Philippe Jaenada, Justine Haenel, Mélois and Prudhomme, and the jury chose Jaenada, who is sixty-two, for "L'Inconnue du quai de Javel". He follows Laurent Mauvignier, whose "La Maison vide" won last year. Speaking on France Inter, Jaenada said it felt really like a kind of vertigo, and described a mixture of joy and emotion.

The Guardian describes the book as a true crime novel, though it is really a literary investigation. It looks into the murder in 1949 of Louise Cansot, a Breton woman who worked as a life model in Paris. Jaenada tries to solve a case now seventy-seven years old, and also to restore the reputation of the victim. I thought that might appeal to you, as it is history told through the patient, human voice of a novelist.

Staying with stories, there is a fond anniversary in the world of comics. Franceinfo notes that Lucky Luke, the cowboy who shoots faster than his own shadow, is eighty years old and still in fine form. Blake and Mortimer reach the same age this year, so two much-loved bande dessinée series are celebrating together. And for thriller lovers, The Guardian has reviewed the fourth season of Lupin on Netflix. The critic calls Omar Sy ridiculously watchable and effortlessly charming as the gentleman thief, and praises the twisty writing and the strong ensemble cast.

Now to schools, where the week has been lively. On Tuesday, after the two weeks of Toussaint holidays, students blockaded dozens of lycées and universities across France. The Local France explains that they are rejecting proposed government education reforms, though turnout was lower than on earlier blockade days. Franceinfo adds that in some schools the protest is being combined with resumed lessons, so the picture varies from place to place. Some pupils are worried, and one is quoted as saying he is very stressed about the bac, concerned about what all this disruption will do to their preparation.

On the official side, the Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has repeated that he is ready to meet representatives of the lycéens next week. Several school and student organisations are continuing their movement in the meantime, so it may be a story to keep half an eye on in the staff room.

One more education note, on teaching resources. Franceinfo reports that the Île-de-France region is still offering digital school textbooks very similar to its withdrawn "manuels libres", even though a court ruling required their removal. Private publishers are complaining about it. It will mostly matter to colleagues who choose resources, but it is a reminder that even textbooks can be a battleground.

On to health and daily life, where there is some more hopeful news. The Local France reports that from the third of November, almost three thousand young doctors are taking up posts in areas short of medical care, many of them in rural France. The idea is simple: that patients can get appointments more easily. And last night on France 5, the programme Enquête de santé broadcast "Migraine, la fin du casse-tête ?", following a pioneering clinical trial at the university hospital in Clermont-Ferrand. It is described as unique in the world, and it raises real hopes for the roughly eleven million people in France who live with migraine. If you missed it, it may be worth looking for on replay.

For a touch of wonder, there is some news from space. Today, Wednesday the fourth of November, the European probe Hera arrives at the asteroid system that NASA's DART probe struck on purpose in twenty twenty-two. That impact was the first test of its kind of planetary defence, a deliberate nudge to an asteroid to see whether it could be moved. Hera's job is to look at the aftermath and answer a lovely, simple question: did the impact leave a crater? It is rather like a detective arriving at the scene, a couple of years after the event.

Finally, three small pieces about language from The Local France, which seem made for a teacher's notebook. The word of the day is "cauchemardesque", meaning nightmarish, offered for anyone who wants to add a little theatrical drama to their complaints. A day of blockades and bac worries might indeed qualify, though I hope yours is gentler. Then there is the expression "vis-à-vis", which turns up in everyday conversation, at work, in the news and in property listings, and which has a wider range of uses than its English cousin. And lastly the idiom "être à couteaux tirés", literally to be at drawn knives, which the press uses when relations are hostile. It is a vivid image, and I suspect your pupils would enjoy comparing it with English equivalents.

That is all for this morning, Yamuna, and I hope your day brings plenty of good sentences and no knives drawn at all.

Good morning, Yamuna. Here is your gentle look at France over the last two days: a literary prize with a story worth stepping into, a lively week in the lycées, some hopeful news about health, a little wonder from space, and a few good words to take away.

Let us begin with books, since the biggest news of the week is from your world. On Tuesday, the Prix Goncourt for twenty twenty-six was awarded, and the winner is Philippe Jaenada, aged sixty-two, for his novel L'Inconnue du quai de Javel. The jury met in Paris and chose from four finalists, with the announcement due from a quarter to one in the afternoon. Alongside Jaenada, the shortlist carried the names of Haenel, Mélois and Prudhomme. He succeeds Laurent Mauvignier, whose novel La Maison vide took the prize last year.

What makes this particular winner interesting for you is the kind of book it is. The Guardian describes it as a true crime novel, though that label sounds a little narrow. It is a literary investigation into a murder that took place in nineteen forty-nine. The victim was Louise Cansot, a Breton woman who worked in Paris as a life model, the sort of person who sat still for painters and sculptors while others made the art. Jaenada sets out to solve a case that is now seventy-seven years old, and, just as importantly, to restore the reputation of a woman whose name had been tarnished. So it is a thriller, a piece of history and an act of quiet justice, all in one. I think that is a rather lovely combination, and it sits very close to your taste for novels that teach the past better than a history essay can. There is even a faint link with painting, in that the heroine of the story earned her living by posing for artists.

Speaking to France Inter after the news, Jaenada said that it really feels like vertigo, using the French word vertige. He described a feeling of joy and of deep emotion at being honoured in this way. It is a good phrase for the dizzy moment when a long, patient piece of work is suddenly lifted up for the whole country to see. If you are looking for something to put in your bag for the winter evenings by the stove in Les Adrets, this may well be it.

Now to schools, which is where much of the French news has been this week, and where I suspect you will have the keenest professional interest. The Toussaint holidays are over, and the lycéens have returned to a movement that began before the break. According to The Local France, on Tuesday the third of November students blockaded dozens of high schools and universities across the country. They are rejecting proposed government education reforms. The report notes that turnout was lower than on earlier blockade days, so the energy of the movement may be shifting, though it is certainly not over.

Franceinfo gives a closer look at what this feels like from the pupils' side. Lycée pupils continued their mobilisation on Tuesday after two weeks of holiday, and in some schools the protest and the lessons are being combined, with classes resuming even as the movement goes on. That sounds like a delicate balance, and not every student is comfortable with it. Several of them told franceinfo that they are anxious about how all this disruption will affect their preparation for the baccalauréat. One of them put it very simply: I am very stressed about the bac. It is a reminder that behind the slogans and the blockades there are young people who are also worrying about their own revision timetables, which will no doubt sound familiar from your own classroom.

On the official side, franceinfo reports that after the holidays several school and student organisations are keeping the movement going, and the Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has repeated that he is ready to meet representatives of the lycéens next week. So there is at least the prospect of a conversation at the highest level. We will see over the coming days whether that meeting takes place and whether it changes the mood in the schools.

There is one more education story, a rather more technical one, but it touches on how teachers choose their materials. Franceinfo reports that the Île-de-France region is still offering digital school textbooks very similar to its so-called manuels libres, the free textbooks that had to be withdrawn after a court ruling. Private publishers are complaining that this continues despite the court's decision. It is a quarrel about who provides what to lycées, and it matters mainly because it affects the resources available to teachers and pupils in the region. It does not concern the Grenoble area directly, but it is the sort of thing colleagues might mention in the staff room.

Let us move to health, where there is some genuinely encouraging news. The Local France reports that from the third of November, almost three thousand young doctors are taking up posts in areas that are short of medical care. Many of these are in rural France. The aim is simple and human: to make it easier for patients in the so-called medical deserts to get an appointment. For anyone who lives in or near the mountains and the smaller villages, where distances to a doctor can be considerable, it is welcome to hear of new faces arriving in those places. It is only a start, of course, but a hopeful one.

On a related note, last night at five past nine on France 5, the programme Enquête de santé broadcast a film titled Migraine, la fin du casse-tête, which you might translate as Migraine, the end of the headache, or perhaps the end of the puzzle, since casse-tête carries both meanings. The film follows a pioneering clinical trial at the university hospital in Clermont-Ferrand, described by franceinfo as unique in the world. About eleven million people in France live with migraine, so the hopes raised by this research are real and widely shared. If you know anyone who suffers, it may be worth mentioning, though I would not want to promise anything beyond what the trial itself shows.

Now, something to lift the eyes upwards. Today, Wednesday the fourth of November, the European space probe Hera arrives at the asteroid system it has been travelling towards. Its task is to examine what happened after NASA's DART probe was deliberately crashed into an asteroid in twenty twenty-two. That impact was the first test of planetary defence of its kind, an attempt to see whether we could nudge a space rock off its path. Franceinfo asks the question that Hera will now try to answer: did the impact produce a crater? It is a lovely question, because the answer may be yes, or it may be that the surface behaved in some way nobody expected. There is something quite poetic about a small machine sent across space to look at the scar left by another small machine. It makes for good thoughts over a morning coffee.

For something lighter on the screen and on the page, there are two items about much-loved characters. The Guardian has reviewed the fourth season of Lupin on Netflix, and the reviewer is clearly delighted. Omar Sy returns as the gentleman thief, and the review calls him ridiculously watchable and effortlessly charming, a blindingly brilliant thief. The praise goes to the twisty writing and to the ensemble cast as well as to the lead. If you enjoy a thriller built around a strong character, and especially one that grew from a fictional hero created more than a century ago, this may be an enjoyable evening or two. As for the character himself, he is a thief with panache, and that has always been half the pleasure.

And in the world of bande dessinée, franceinfo marks an anniversary. Lucky Luke, the cowboy who shoots faster than his own shadow, is eighty years old, and the piece says he is still in fine form, bon pied, bon œil, as the French say, meaning sprightly and sharp-eyed. Blake and Mortimer, the other great series of the Franco-Belgian tradition, also turn eighty this year. So two long-running heroes, one in the Wild West and one in the world of English gentlemen adventurers, share a birthday. It is a happy little cultural item, and perhaps a nice excuse to look again at some old albums, or to put one in the hands of a pupil who thinks comics are only for children.

Finally, a few words for a linguist. The Local France has three small language pieces this week, and they are rather good company for each other. The word of the day is cauchemardesque, which means nightmarish. The Local suggests it is ideal for anyone who wants to add a little theatrical drama to a complaint. So the traffic on the road down to Grenoble can be cauchemardesque, as can a pile of marking, though I suspect you would find a better use for it in a novel. It is a word with a pleasing sound, a long, rolling shape, and it carries the French cauchemar, nightmare, inside it.

The expression of the day is vis-à-vis. The Local explains that it turns up all over French life: in ordinary conversation, in the workplace, in political news and even in property listings. Its range is wider than that of the English phrase we borrowed from it. In English we tend to say vis-à-vis rather grandly, to mean in relation to or compared with. In French it can also be about literally facing something, as in a house opposite another house, which is why it appears in estate agents' language. It is a small lesson in how a word can travel and change its coat on the way.

And the second expression is être à couteaux tirés, which literally means to be at drawn knives. The press uses it when relations between people or groups are hostile. It is a vivid image, and a handy one for a language class. Pupils tend to remember an idiom better when they can picture it, and it would not be hard to picture two parties glaring at each other with blades out. It also stands as a gentle contrast to the more civilised conversation that the Prime Minister says he hopes to have with the lycéens next week.

That is your France for this morning, Yamuna, and I hope the day brings you a good book, a good word and a clear view of the sky.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Wednesday the fourth of November, and the last two days have brought a good run of stories: prizes for writers, repair after old wounds, and some very hopeful news from the natural world.

Let me begin with books, since the biggest literary news is French. On Tuesday, Philippe Jaenada, who is sixty-two, won the Prix Goncourt for his novel L'Inconnue du quai de Javel. Franceinfo reports that he spoke on France Inter soon afterwards, and the phrase he chose was that it felt like a vertigo, a kind of dizziness. He talked about joy and emotion, which is rather lovely to hear from a writer at that moment. The Guardian adds the detail that makes the book so appealing. It is a literary investigation into the murder in 1949 of Louise Cansot, a Breton woman who worked as a life model in Paris. Jaenada sets out to solve a case that is now seventy-seven years old, and also to restore the reputation of the victim, who had been judged unfairly. That is a thriller and a work of history in one, with a real woman at its heart. I think it's exactly the sort of book that teaches the texture of a period better than any textbook, because the investigator is present on the page, following leads and doubting himself, and the reader walks alongside him.

Staying with the written word, the poet Grace Nichols has won the Royal Society of Literature's Pioneer prize, worth ten thousand pounds. The prize honours women writers over sixty who broke barriers, and The Guardian quotes the description of her as a trailblazer in the truest sense. Nichols was born in Guyana and is based in Britain, and she is best known for I Is a Long-Memoried Woman, a collection in which the voice of memory is so strong that you hear it as much as read it. If you ever want a poem that sounds wonderful read aloud with a class, she is a fine place to look, and it is good to see her recognised in this way.

And there is a little gem from Upworthy that belongs with the books, even though it isn't one. A Japanese man has shared the diary his sister kept in 1998, when she was sixteen and spending a year as an exchange student in Iowa. The extract has a wonderfully observant young narrator, and what makes it special is its quiet detail. She writes about people waving to strangers on the road, a small, unfamiliar gesture that a newcomer notices and a local would never think about. It has a personal, almost literary feel, and it made me think of how often the best narrators are people looking at an ordinary world with fresh eyes. You might even find a use for it with your première students, as a model of voice and attention to small things.

From pages to canvases now. At Tate St Ives, a retrospective of the British modernist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham has opened, and The Guardian has a long piece about it. At the centre of the show hangs her large painting Glacier, Blue Cave. Barns-Graham was an artist long sidelined in the story that gets told about St Ives and its painters, and this exhibition sets about correcting that. The article describes how her work drew on glaciers, on Vietnam, and on the end of her own marriage, so that landscape and private life run together in the paintings. It's a good reminder of how an image can carry grief and wonder at the same time, and it makes for a fine companion to a poem about ice or light.

Let me turn now to two stories about history and repair, both of which read almost like novels. The first comes from Upworthy. During the Second World War, the maharaja Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja took in around one thousand Polish children and recreated a home for them on Indian soil. Think about what that means. These were children who had lost their country, and a ruler on the other side of the world decided that they should not also lose their sense of who they were. It is a story of rescue, but also of identity, of how you keep a language and a culture alive far from where it began. There's a novel in there, and I rather hope someone writes it, if they haven't already.

The second story, from Good News Network, is quieter and very moving. In Punjab, Sikhs and Hindus are organising the rebuilding of old mosques that were destroyed after Partition, while Muslims look on. Much of the effort is led by people who remember the violence themselves, which gives it an extra weight. They are not rebuilding out of abstract principle, but as a way of mending something they saw broken. Partition is a subject that literature has handled with great power, and this is a living sequel of sorts, an account of what some people choose to do with their memories decades later. It is a real, concrete act of reconciliation, brick by brick.

On a related note about how we look after each other, Positive News has a thoughtful piece about a village in England that has set up a social care community. Instead of treating care as a service delivered to people from outside, it is built around communal living and shared responsibility. The article asks what would happen if we stopped thinking of social care as a service at all, and whether this model could spread elsewhere. I like that it begins with a question rather than a promise. It's a gentle read about neighbourliness and what it might look like if it were organised properly, not left to chance.

Health next, and some hope for a very common condition. Franceinfo reports on a clinical trial at the CHU of Clermont-Ferrand, described as unique in the world, which is looking at the treatment of migraine. Last night at five past nine on France 5, the programme Enquête de santé broadcast a film called Migraine, la fin du casse-tête, following the trial. About eleven million people in France live with migraine, so the hopes raised by this work are far from small. The trial is still a trial, so nobody is promising a cure, but it's good to see serious, pioneering research happening in France and being explained to the public. If you or anyone you know suffers, it may be worth looking out for a replay.

Now to the natural world, where there is a particularly rich harvest today. Starting in Australia, The Optimist Daily reports that New South Wales has created the Great Koala National Park, now the state's second-largest national park. It took more than a decade of campaigning and three state elections to get there, which is a lesson in persistence. The piece also explains how carbon credits helped make it possible, which is a concrete detail about how conservation can actually be paid for. For the koalas, this means protected habitat, and for everyone else it's evidence that long campaigns can succeed.

Closer to home, or at least closer to the English-speaking world, Good News Network says that beavers are about to return to the area around Loch Ness. They were last recorded there between fifteen twenty-six and fifteen twenty-seven, so this is a return after roughly five hundred years. The article calls them ecosystem engineers, because the dams and pools they build reshape the land and create homes for many other creatures. And there is something irresistibly funny about Loch Ness welcoming a new monster, in the shape of a beaver. It is natural history with a light touch, and I suspect the original monster would be quite pleased with the company.

Under the sea, there is a piece of research from Stanford that offers real encouragement. The Optimist Daily reports that scientists there found that bleached coral can heal through touch. A fragment of bleached coral began to recover within days after it was placed touching a healthy one. The healthy coral passed along the symbiotic algae that the bleached one had lost, and those algae are what give coral both its colour and its life. Bleaching has been one of the most worrying stories about the oceans for years, so a finding like this, simple and observable, is welcome. It is early science, and I would not want to overstate it, but the image of one coral quite literally helping another to recover is a striking one.

And from the sea to the stars. Astronomers have identified what is described as the first green star, according to The Optimist Daily, and the article links it to chemistry left behind by a dead planet. I don't have more of the technical detail than that, but the image is a wonderful one: a green point of light in the night sky, shining because of what remains of a world that no longer exists. It is the sort of thing a poet would seize upon, and a good example of how science can hand us language as well as facts.

One more nature story, with a very modern twist. The Optimist Daily has profiled Maya Higa as part of its Local Changemakers 2026 series. She built a wildlife sanctuary on Twitch, funded by the people who watch it. The piece opens with her refusing to swim with sperm whales in Dominica, a memorable way to begin, because it tells you straight away that she cares more about the animals than about the spectacle. It's a story about how an online audience can be turned into practical support for conservation, which is not something many of us would have predicted.

Last of all, something purely joyful. Upworthy shares a short video of the Gardiner Brothers performing Irish step dance to Beyoncé's country song Texas Hold 'Em. Two brothers, quick feet, and a song you would never expect to hear alongside that kind of dancing, and yet it works beautifully. Given your fondness for dance and music, I thought it might brighten a break between lessons, and it needs only a minute or two of your time.

That is all for today, Yamuna, and I hope you find something here to carry with you on the way down into the valley, whether it's a beaver, a green star or a waving stranger on an Iowa road.
