briefing.text:
Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Wednesday.

Let me begin with books, since there's good news from the Prix Goncourt. Philippe Jaenada, aged sixty-two, won on Tuesday for "L'Inconnue du quai de Javel". Speaking on France Inter, he described a feeling of joy and emotion, and franceinfo quotes him saying it really feels like a vertigo. The Guardian describes the book as a literary investigation into the murder in nineteen forty-nine of Louise Cansot, a Breton woman who worked as a life model in Paris. It tries to solve a case now seventy-seven years old, and to restore the victim's reputation. That is history told through a novel, and rather close to your heart.

Staying with writers, the poet Grace Nichols, born in Guyana and based in Britain, has won the Royal Society of Literature's Pioneer prize, worth ten thousand pounds. It honours women writers over sixty who broke barriers, and the Guardian calls her a trailblazer in the truest sense. You may know her for "I Is a Long-Memoried Woman", a title that sings all by itself. Also, the Los Angeles Review of Books has a piece on Olga Tokarczuk's "Primeval and Other Times". She is a writer of lyrical, widely ranging fiction, so it may be worth a look for the shape of the book as much as its story.

Now to painting and music. The Guardian has a rapturous review of the V&A's exhibition in London, "Constantinople to Istanbul". It brings together Byzantine and Ottoman treasures from one great city, and the critic says you won't want to leave. London is a long way from Les Adrets, but the review alone is a pleasure. On a similar theme of connections, the National Gallery has a short video with Megan Renoir, great-great-granddaughter of Pierre-Auguste Renoir. She talks behind the scenes about the exhibition "Renoir and Love", and offers a personal glimpse of the painter's way of living in the moment.

And on BBC Radio 4, Front Row has a forty-two-minute episode on "Orbiting Orbital". This is a composition by Nitin Sawhney inspired by Samantha Harvey's Booker-winning novel "Orbital", with new writing by Harvey herself. The same programme covers a biography of Michael Gambon and the Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at the Design Museum.

Closer to home, there are two evenings you might enjoy. Tonight, at eight o'clock, the Théâtre Hexagone in Meylan stages "SOIF", a piece of about an hour and twenty minutes by Bougier Toto. It explores belief within contemporary knowledge, and also water and memory. One further date is listed, if tonight doesn't suit. And on Friday, the sixth of November, at seven in the evening, Compagnie Caminos performs Shipibo tales at the Espace Aragon in Villard-Bonnot. It is an evening of oral tradition, storytelling in the old sense, which should appeal to anyone who loves a strong narrative voice.

For some good news, Upworthy tells the story of a maharaja, Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja, who during the Second World War took in around a thousand Polish children and recreated a home for them on Indian soil. It is a story of rescue and identity that reads like a novel. And from Positive News, a village in England has set up a social care community built on communal living and shared responsibility rather than a conventional service. The piece asks whether the model could spread, and it's a thoughtful read on how people look after one another.

If you're in the mood to watch something, Arte has a documentary, "Vivre en Ukraine, en guerre". It is wordless and hypnotic, with wide shots of Kyiv, the front line and ordinary lives, including the moment a statue of Soviet friendship is toppled. It's a quiet, unsparing portrait of a nation changed by war, and it's available until the tenth of December. For something grander, the Royal Opera has released a trailer for its Tosca, directed by Oliver Mears. Aleksandra Kurzak, Saimir Pirgu and Christopher Maltman lead the cast, with Daniel Oren conducting. It is Puccini's opera as a thriller: love, police intrigue and a dreadful bargain.

Finally, a small corner for the BFI. Ben Okri turns up twice. The Spectator has him discussing the power of the short novel, though all I have is the headline, so I can't say more about his argument. The Observer, meanwhile, looks at how he turns to the myths of the past to respond to the present. That headline is cut short too, but given his love of folklore and storytelling, it may offer something for the classroom. And for the oral themes list, the Edinburgh Reporter has given a two-star review of a production of "1984". Again I only have the headline, so I can't tell you which production, but Orwell is on your list, so it's worth knowing about.

That is your morning, Yamuna. I hope your day is full of good sentences and good stories.
